title: Replacing the webbing on a vintage deck chair
subtitle: Strip old rotted canvas and reweave a deck chair with new cotton or acrylic replacement webbing
excerpt: How to strip and replace the woven seat webbing on a wooden deck chair. Covers removing the old canvas, preparing the frame, cutting and weaving new webbing through the rails, and securing the ends.
sourceNotes: Traditional deck chair construction practice. UK deckchair canvas replacement guides (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: The woven seat material of a deck chair. Traditional material is a lightly woven cotton canvas, typically 40 to 50 mm wide and hemmed at the edges. The webbing wraps around the back rail and the front rail and is secured at each end by tacks or staples. Modern replacement webbing in acrylic is more weather-resistant than cotton and is the preferred choice for an outdoor chair.

content.text: is stapled or tacked to the back and front rails and wraps around the frame. Replacing it restores a deck chair that is in good structural condition but has perished canvas. Acrylic webbing lasts significantly longer than cotton in outdoor conditions.

Fold the chair flat to access the fixing points on the top and bottom rails. Use the staple remover to lift staples or the tack hammer to pull out tacks. Cut through the webbing at the centre with the utility knife and unthread it from the frame. Clean any rust marks from the rails with a light sanding and apply a coat of exterior wood treatment if the timber is bare.

Measure the total length needed for a single run: the seat depth from the top edge of the back rail to the top edge of the front rail, plus 100 mm at each end for the turn-under and fixing allowance. A standard seat is approximately 400 mm deep; add 200 mm for the total webbing run. Multiply by the number of runs (a standard chair uses 3 to 5 runs side by side, separated by a small gap). Cut all strips from the webbing roll with the upholstery shears.

Fold 50 mm of webbing back over itself at one end to form a double thickness. Lay this folded end over the top rail (the back of the seat) with the fold facing down and the webbing running forward. Staple through both layers into the top face of the rail with three or four 10 mm T50 staples across the width of the webbing. Keep the staples in from the edge of the rail.
Run the webbing and fix the second end

Run the webbing over the seat frame and over the front rail. Pull it firmly so the seat will be taut under a seated weight but not so tight that the frame bows. Fold 50 mm back over the front rail and staple in the same way as the back. Repeat for each parallel run of webbing, keeping the spacing even. On traditional wide-canvas deck chairs, the single canvas is stapled to both rails in the same way: fold the canvas around the back rail, staple, pull forward over the frame, fold around the front rail, and staple.

attrs.symptom: Webbing sags significantly after one season
attrs.cause: Cotton webbing stretches in wet conditions; canvas was not pulled tight enough on fitting.
attrs.fix: Replace cotton webbing with acrylic. When fitting, pull the webbing noticeably tighter than feels correct: acrylic stretches slightly under the first loading.

attrs.symptom: Staples pulling out of the rail at one end
attrs.cause: Rail timber is soft or end-grain timber was used for the rail.
attrs.fix: Use tacks instead of staples on soft or end-grain timber: drive upholstery tacks at a slight angle and punch the heads home with the tack hammer.
